Sweet cream ice cream. It just milk and sugar.

Yes, it does exist, but it's pretty hard to find because it tends to be made specifically to showcase extremely high quality cream, such as Cornish clotted cream. These kinds of products are usually limited to a small (often tourist based) regional market. I believe I'm correct in saying that you can find it in Tillamook, Oregon.

The best way to approach what you want to do would be an ice cream making machine. They can be found online, and they're usually about the size of a blender. You just add your own cream, milk, sugar, and flavorings.

Not sure where you live, but I am very picky over chocolste milkshakes. It has to be made with chocolate icecream, not vanilla ice cream with syrup. Everyone uses Hershey's syrup. Once you do that, they all taste the same.

So when I go to a new icecream shop, I ask how they are made. I went to Whitey's in Davenport Iowa and they said that they use a flavorless icecream and put syrup and malt in it. So if you ask, there may be someone that uses it near you.

It would not be difficult to make what you need, simply by omitting vanilla from a standard vanilla ice cream recipe. My "go to" basic ice cream is Fanny Cradock's standard recipe, which you can find in the "Daily Telegraph Sociable Cook's Book" (Collins Fontana Books, 1967) by "Bon Viveur" (a pen name used by Fanny and Johnny Cradock). The recipe in this book uses a standard confectioners' custard, for which the recipe is found in the "Daily Telegraph Cook's Book" (Collins Fontana Books, 1964), also by Bon Viveur. Note that when making the custard for ice cream you should omit the tiny quantity of cornflour from the custard recipe. Both these recipes are, in my experience, almost failure-proof. (I have only had the custard curdle twice in more than ten years of using them, and both times it was my fault.) The basic recipes Fanny Cradock provides are extremely easy, but you can use them as the base for all sorts of experiments. I've had huge success using the ice cream base for a wide range of flavours, including most fruit, chocolate, coffee, brown bread, ginger and angelica. Good luck!
Oh, and banana. Make banana ice cream on this base, churn it well, and people will talk about it for years afterwards!
